---
title: "Learning from a sample"
---

An empirical proportion depends on which units receive equal weight. A token proportion weights every retained token equally. An average of speaker proportions first weights tokens within speaker and then weights speakers equally. These are different weighting schemes, and they may target different quantities because their denominators represent different units.

Neither summary is automatically a population quantity. If the research question concerns speakers in a region, the population includes speakers who did not contribute to the corpus. The question for this module is thus not merely how to calculate a sample summary. It is: what can the observed speakers and clauses tell us about a specified quantity in a specified population?

The module first fixes populations, samples, and estimator behavior; it then develops frequentist interval and test procedures, introduces Bayesian updating and prediction, and finally builds the computational and diagnostic tools needed when posterior calculations are not available in closed form.

## What you should already know

This module assumes the distinction between a [linguistic unit and its observation key](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd#unit-and-observation-key), between a [random variable and its realized value](../random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd#distinguishing-the-two-spaces), and between [independence and factorization](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent). It also uses [expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) and the [variance--covariance decomposition](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#covariance-and-a-variance-decomposition).

Three datasets recur. UD Turkish BOUN supplies token and sentence units for likelihood and sampling questions. Hillenbrand vowel durations supply speaker-level acoustic measurements for estimator and interval questions. UniMorph Turkish supplies lexeme--paradigm cells for finite-resource and Bayesian examples. The later computational sequence uses 55 aggregated Provo passage contrasts; its canonical data and model description is the [nonconjugate-model page](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#a-robust-location-scale-model).

## Populations, samples, and estimators

We begin by distinguishing [populations from samples](populations-and-samples.qmd). The population must identify the units to which the claim applies, while the sample contains the units that were observed. An [independent sampling model](independent-sampling.qmd) then states how repeated observations are related to a population parameter.

The [pronoun case example](pronoun-case-example.qmd) uses a binomial model for one corpus proportion. [Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) selects the parameter value that assigns the greatest probability to the observed sample. An [estimator](properties-of-estimators.qmd) is the rule that maps each possible sample to an estimate, while the estimate is the value obtained from the realized sample.

The sampling distribution of an estimator allows us to define its [standard error](standard-errors.qmd), [bias](estimator-bias.qmd), and [mean squared error](mean-squared-error.qmd). [Confidence intervals](confidence-intervals.qmd) and [exact binomial intervals](exact-binomial-intervals.qmd) are procedures whose coverage is defined across repeated samples. [Null hypotheses and test statistics](null-hypotheses-and-test-statistics.qmd) compare an observed statistic with a reference distribution under a stated null hypothesis.

Later pages apply these definitions in increasing order of design complexity: first to one mean, then to paired acoustic measurements, then to two independent means, and finally to contingency tables. In each case, we will name the independent unit before calculating an interval or test.

## Updating uncertainty with Bayes' rule

Bayesian inference begins with a probability model for the observations and adds a probability distribution over unknown parameters. The [posterior distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd) uses Bayes' rule to combine a prior distribution and likelihood. The [posterior summaries page](posterior-summaries.qmd) then asks which features of that distribution address a particular linguistic claim.

Some posterior distributions can be calculated algebraically. [Conjugate priors](conjugate-priors.qmd) make one class of such calculations possible by keeping the posterior in a known family.

The next distinction concerns prediction. A [prior predictive distribution](prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) states what the model predicts before the present observations update it, while a [posterior predictive distribution](predictive-distributions.qmd) states what it predicts after that update. Both distributions put the prediction on an observable response scale. [Other models](beyond-conjugacy.qmd) leave a posterior that is mathematically defined but not available as a familiar normalized formula. We thus begin with a finite update, summarize it, derive a conjugate update, predict before and after conditioning, and only then turn to numerical approximation. This order keeps the inferential target separate from the algorithm used to approximate it.

## Posterior computation and checking

The computational sequence also has an order. [Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd) first explains why averages of target draws approximate expectations. [Importance sampling](importance-sampling.qmd) changes the distribution used to produce those draws. [Markov chains](markov-chains.qmd) and [Markov chain Monte Carlo](markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd) then permit dependent draws when direct independent sampling is unavailable.

The remaining pages move from Metropolis-Hastings transitions to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Stan's implementation. Only after the sampler has been defined do we read trace plots, $\widehat R$, autocorrelation, [effective sample size](effective-sample-size.qmd), divergences, and parameter pairs. Effective sample size translates dependence among simulation draws into an independent-draw count with comparable numerical precision. [Generated quantities](generated-quantities.qmd) and [posterior predictive checks](posterior-predictive-checks.qmd) then return us to the response scale. This final return matters: a sampler may accurately approximate a posterior for a model that predicts the linguistic data poorly.

The concept pages sometimes preview a later implementation: the Markov-chain and MCMC pages state the symmetric accept--reject transition locally before its detailed MH derivation, the HMC page links forward to the full mass-matrix treatment when it whitens coordinates, and the NUTS page labels its stored Stan diagnostics as a preview of the exact program. These forward references are deliberate; no displayed computation should depend on an unnamed device.

For each inferential result, identify the population quantity, the sampling or observation model, and the procedure that maps the realized sample to the reported value. A token proportion, an average speaker proportion, and a regional population proportion remain three different quantities even when they are calculated from the same file.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) shows the probability concepts used in this module. We assume the earlier definitions of [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd), [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd), [expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd), and [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd). Begin with [populations and samples](populations-and-samples.qmd).

## Module recap

1. Name the population, unit, estimand, and sampling or observation model before choosing a procedure.
2. Keep random estimators and intervals distinct from their realized numerical values.
3. Posterior computation approximates a declared model; the empirical evidence remains the observations supplied to that model.
4. End on the response scale by checking the implications that matter for the linguistic claim.
